body.text: Some 45 years have passed since this writer first saw that breathtaking film about how “untouchables” lived and died—in poverty, squalor, and abject degradation—once upon a time in the land that now goes by the name of Gujarat. It was a cold January day, and the venue of the screening, as a part of the Indian Panorama showcase, was Mavalankar Auditorium on Rafi Marg in New Delhi. Bhavni Bhavai (1981) left the audience speechless with its then 28-year-old director Ketan Mehta’s formidably innovative style, challenging formal experimentation, visual richness, hilariously energetic performances, and its deeply moving folkloric narrative. Radical as much in its form as in its politics, Bhavni Bhavai was the kind of iconic achievement that any director, however distinguished, would be hard put to repeat. Understandably, Mehta’s subsequent career was never to soar like it did with his first film.

Untouchability may not have the same severe external face in Gujarat today as it existed in earlier times, but the curse is still very much there, as proved by a series of atrocities recently committed in the name of caste, against women in particular. If the entire State is to be faulted on this count, it is in the northern part that lawlessness prevails the most. While village elders go about policing society, reminiscent of the role of khap panchayats in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, or Rajasthan, the keepers of law habitually look the other way. Meanwhile, it is uncommon for the media to report atrocities against Dalits. As the malaise grows by the day, so does the reality of caste and Hindu society being one indivisible whole.

In fact, with Hindutva enjoying an unassailable position in Gujarat for the past three decades or so, proved most recently by BJP victories in local body elections, there is an alarming spurt in Manuvad, which argues for Brahmin supremacy in every sphere of society. At such a time, when the forces of orthodoxy and obscurantism are being allowed to have a field day even as the religious Right is keen to project Gujarat as an all-round success story, the relevance of a delicate yet stout human document like Bhavni Bhavai cannot be overemphasised.

Perhaps it would be in order to explore, however sketchily, the history of Gujarati cinema prior to the appearance of Bhavni Bhavai—for one thing, to establish the historical significance of Mehta’s film. Disappointingly, Gujarati cinema has traditionally been largely escapist in nature, “feverishly pursuing mythological, religious and legendary themes”, to quote Kantilal Rathod, director of Kanku, which remains to this day one of the handful of meaningful films to have been made in Gujarati. In this context, it is strange that Gujarati cinema should have carried such a dismal face, considering the pioneering efforts by Gujarati producers active in the Bombay film industry since the 1920s. In contrast, Marathi films emerging out of a neighbouring space have shown a marked interest in subjects of social concern, fleshed out in styles that seemed quite advanced at times.
Roots in theatre and a formative encounter

Even while keeping in mind that literature and cinema are quite dissimilar forms of artistic expression and many great films have been known to have non-literary origins, perhaps one of the reasons for Gujarati cinema’s ill-health lies in the lack of interest shown by filmmakers in novels and short stories with contemporary themes and rich in human values. This was clearly stated by Rathod and other directors like Kanti Madia, Govind Saraiya, or Upendra Trivedi. In fact, of the 150 films made in Gujarati till 1975, only a handful were based on well-known literary texts, notably Kanku, written by Pannalal Patel, Prithvi vallabh by K.M. Munshi, and Gunsundari No Ghar Sansar by Goverdhanram Tripathi.

Another reason, arguably a more plausible one, why Gujarati cinema is still to attain a semblance of maturity is its obvious dependence on Bombay extravaganzas for “inspiration”. Hindi formula films have long cast their baneful shadow on Gujarati films in a big way, in the same way in which they have polluted, in varying degrees, other bhasha cinemas in the country. Stunt films packed with dance items, or vulgar displays of sex and violence exceeding all levels of endurance, never cease to increase in number or grow in popularity with viewers wanting to keep away from their real, deprived lives.

Having said such (deservedly) unkind things about Gujarati cinema in general, it is in the fitness of things that the balance needs to be righted with the kind of high praise that a rare gem like Bhavni Bhavai deserves. This writer had observed in Motif, the Jamshedpur avant-garde weekly paper, on March 30, 1981: “If Gujarati cinema is to start being relevant and meaningful, it must, so to say, clasp to its bosom and encourage in all possible ways a rare talent like Ketan Mehta.”

A film like Bhavni Bhavai couldn’t have happened in a day. Even as Mehta was studying for a degree in economics at St. Stephen’s College, Delhi, he immersed himself in books, films, theatre, and other artistic and intellectual spaces, especially theatre, which seems to have held him in a lifelong thrall. In the past three decades of the last century, the national capital saw the arrival and departure of several theatre personalities who left behind their imprints on many gifted young minds wanting to do something new, something different. Ketan Mehta was among those who sought out geniuses like B.V. Karanth and rising stars like M.K. Raina. He read Bertolt Brecht deeply, as well as texts on Japanese theatrical traditions, including Kabuki and Noh. As things turned out, he was to benefit immensely from these readings when he came to make his first film.

Following Delhi, Mehta’s next port of call was Poona, where he studied direction at the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII). While he was not a direct student of Ritwik Ghatak, Mehta did have the opportunity to meet the maestro once. About that meeting, Mehta is on record: “I met him only once, when he had come to do a workshop over four days at the film institute. This was sometime in the early 1970s, well after he had retired from his position as vice-principal. That brief interaction left a deep impact on me, and on my film-making too. The dramatic and charged emotional content of his films leaves an impression on anyone watching, shaking them up profoundly, making them question their very existence—that, I think, is a very strong element of Ritwikda’s films.” (Ref: Unmechanical—Ritwik Ghatak in 50 Fragments, ed. by Shamya Dasgupta, 2025).

Coming to think of it, when you have a great teacher like Ghatak interacting with a keen and precociously gifted student like Ketan Mehta, even if it is for just four days, it could well end up as a lifetime of experiencing the unforgettable for the latter. As much can be read into Mehta’s memorialising of the encounter. “The workshop wasn’t a film-making course really. It was more like an interaction with him. He was already unwell, and not active as a filmmaker—though he would make a few more films after that before passing away in 1976—but I found his intensity very infectious. His passion for cinema was infectious, his passion for India and Indians was very infectious, and his empathy for all the young film-makers was enchanting. But it was his love for cinema that was, perhaps, my main takeaway from the workshop.”
The garb of the untouchable

Bhavni Bhavai harks back to a time in the history of Gujarat when thousands of people had to wear what was called achhootna vesh (garb of the untouchables). The upper castes imposed on the untouchables certain dress restrictions which were meant not only to subjugate them and keep them in eternal physical bondage but also to defeat them emotionally, terrorise them psychologically, and dehumanise them—to make them appear less than human in their own eyes. What were these instructions? The untouchable had to tie a broom behind his back, which would erase his “offensive footprints”; wear a third sleeve as a mark of submission; wear only unwoven yarn as headgear; and carry a spittoon round his neck so as not to pollute the air or the earth around him. Anyone not following the prescribed code was dealt with severely.

When Asait Thakore, a 14th-century Brahmin dissenter, was found visiting homes of the untouchables and having food with them, he was excommunicated from Brahmin society. Since then, Asait Thakore has been a part of the history of resistance to upper caste tyranny in Gujarat. Ketan Mehta is on record that he was inspired to make Bhavni Bhavai by the teachings and example of Asait Thakore; the art, politics, and theatre of Bertolt Brecht; and the poetics of Noh and Kabuki. That such a composite film-maker, with a sound grounding in theatre, should feel attracted to the cinema of Ritwik Ghatak, who started out as a theatre person himself, is hardly surprising. Mehta: “The dramatic intensity of the narrative (in Bhavni Bhavai) was somewhere influenced by the style of acting in Ritwikda’s films. And basic social consciousness, of course. And yes, the same sort of ethos and logic holds true for (my second film) Mirch Masala (1986) too.”

Arguably, no one in the history of Indian cinema has mounted a more pulsating carnival of music, colour, horseplay, sound and dance, interplay of space, time and movement, and varied modes of storytelling to denounce social obscurantism than what Ketan Mehta did in Bhavni Bhavai. A stylised form of Gujarati folk drama, Bhavai, synthesises diverse performing arts into socially relevant communication. It was used by Mehta with deadly effect to bring home to his audience how society as a whole is weakened and corrupted when any of its parts is unjustly treated. When prejudice and cruelty become the norm in the way the privileged treat those rendered powerless by the machinations of hierarchies, it inevitably leads to conflict ending in a violent reconfiguration of the social system. Mehta is not at all apologetic when he says that though his film was primarily an exercise in art and aesthetics, it was also a call to action. The social and moral responsibilities of art matter to him.

In this regard, it is interesting to read Mehta mentioning Bhavni Bhavai having two alternative climaxes. “One was the traditional end to the folktale (being related by the fireside by the old man), and the other, proposed by someone from the crowd of the old man’s listeners, who doesn’t want to accept the status quo ending, and calls for a rebellious, revolutionary ending.” For all its artistic excellence and the novelty of its aesthetics, a film with such an ending is unlikely to have a screening in present-day Gujarat, held as it is in the vice-like grip of dominant caste traditionalists. Even Mehta, with an almost adulatory film on Vallabhbhai Patel under his belt, is unlikely to have an easy passage with Bhavni Bhavai in his home State, beset as it is by the most extreme kind of polarisation along caste and communal lines, not to forget the notorious disparities between the very rich and the very poor.
A stylist and a moralist

Ketan Mehta has often spoken of how his journey to cinema began via both the street and proscenium theatre, where he picked up his first lessons in not just the poetics of art, but also the moral basis of his creative orientation. In a signed article written for the 1991 Annual Number of Cinema in India, a National Film Development Corporation (NFDC) publication, Mehta observed: “While I was in college, I was active in street theatre. From college, we would go out on the road, into jhuggies (slums) and put up instant, one-act plays against imperialism. At the film institute, I realised that all cinema is political—it either wants change or cunningly maintains the status quo. Every film reflects the ideology of its director, whether he supports justice or evil.”

Perhaps one would not be mistaken if one were to claim that, couched in these words, is Mehta’s wanting to be both a stylist and a moralist of cinema. But with his remarkable intelligence and his insights into what separated an artistic film with a moral basis from one that confused art with propaganda, Mehta distanced himself from doing the morality bit. Poring through the annals of New Indian Cinema, one would be hard put to collect more than a dozen extraordinary efforts remembered to this day by virtue of their successful quest to question the status quo by means of new idioms, new styles, and new aesthetics.

If, starting out in the late 1960s, this more argumentative than creative movement shrivelled up by the beginning of the 1990s, the principal reason for this was the weariness and viewer fatigue caused by the constant moralistic attitudinising on the part of the lion’s share of directors, who appeared to think that the vacuum caused by the absence of logical storytelling by artistic means could be filled by excessive reliance on speechifying and sloganeering. The contest between right and wrong in a Satyajit Ray film, or in a work by Saeed Mirza or Ketan Mehta, would more often than not be played out more in terms of ideas contained in images strung together with an eye to dramaturgical effect.

Soon after Bhavni Bhavai had met with great critical success, both at home and abroad, Mehta said: “In Indian films the alienation of the rural poor from the urban way of life has become clichétic. What we require is some kind of synthesis of the two with our own past and heritage. The purpose of a film should not be to alienate people. I have chosen a popular form (bhavai) so that the people for whom the film is made can understand it. My film traces the history of the social evil of untouchability in Gujarat and what it means today …. Form by itself is not sacrosanct. Different forms are necessary to communicate different messages.”

If anything, these words may be said to be an attempt to show how necessary it is for an intellectual elite to stay clear of the trap called elitism. How often have we seen an otherwise perceptive and well-endowed filmmaker end up in a heap of mangled ambitions when, consumed by over-confidence in his own abilities or, worse still, a certain contempt for lesser mortals, he allows himself to float away in a wave of self-indulgence ending in self-defeating incomprehensibility. The wise man knows the advantages of learning while earning; in other words, the successful artist is he who is able to bring his audience into his embrace without diluting his own standards of innovativeness and creativity.

Bhavni Bhavai is a classic instance of a filmmaker being able to communicate his point of view regarding a long-standing social evil by means that are astonishingly creative and yet understandable to the lowest common denominator. Instead of narcissism and arrogance, so common in the case of so-called artists claiming to be interested in doing something new, Mehta showed a profitable willingness to get off the high horse of the poseur, the intellectual hoity-toity, or the empty propagandist, to create a film that soared even as it refused to divorce itself from the daily experience of the wretched and the wronged.

Perhaps none of Ketan Mehta’s Indian New Wave peers felt more enthused by the success that had come to attend Bhavni Bhavai than Govindan Aravindan (1935-1991). The Malayali auteur, with deep knowledge of several arts from painting to music to theatre, showed his appreciation of his younger contemporary’s debut film thus: “We are, I feel, working with a totally Western idiom (cinema). Using the same techniques and the same chemistry, can we evolve a new form, a new sensibility? Ketan Mehta has tried in Bhavni Bhavai. This is something that we have to try. Using that idiom to evolve a form of our own is not easy.”

If Ketan Mehta had chosen—say, for some unearthly reason—to retire from filmmaking after having made Bhavni Bhavai, he would still have been remembered for long as a major contributor to the making of New Indian Cinema, such was the film’s strength of conviction, which was able to leave its mark precisely because it moved in remarkable tandem with the skills and subtleties of a certain category of high subaltern cinema. One can never get tired of visiting again and again this timeless document about a timeless Indian cancer, tragically incurable however hard the Asait Thakores may try.
